title: Visualizing Distinct Motoneuron Pools in Adult Zebrafish via Retrograde Tracers
author: Bertuzzi, Pallucchi, et al.

steps.title: Anesthetize and secure fish
steps.instruction: Deeply anesthetize each injected zebrafish in 0.1 % MS‑222 solution, place briefly on a paper towel to remove excess water, then glue the fish laterally onto a glass Petri dish with superglue covering head and tail, and immediately submerge the dish in 1× PBS.

steps.title: Dissect to expose vertebrae
steps.instruction: Using surgical tools, remove internal organs, first the skin then the muscle layers, to reveal the vertebrae.

steps.title: Fix tissue in 4% PFA
steps.instruction: Discard the 1× PBS, add 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) to the dish and keep at 4 °C for 2–24 h to achieve optimal fixation.

steps.title: Rinse and prepare for isolation
steps.instruction: After fixation, discard the PFA, rinse once with 1× PBS, and refill the dish with fresh 1× PBS.

steps.title: Isolate spinal cord under microscope
steps.instruction: Under a stereomicroscope, use forceps to remove neural spines (ns) and vertebral arches, then remove hemal spines (hs) and the centrum (c) to expose the spinal cord; transfer the isolated cord to a multi‑well plate containing 1× PBS.

steps.title: Store spinal cord in PBS
steps.instruction: Keep the isolated spinal cords in 1× PBS at 4 °C and complete subsequent steps within 48 h to avoid dextran‑dye degradation.

steps.title: Schedule protocol timeline
steps.instruction: Perform the entire protocol within 10 days; allocate approximately 2 days for the tissue fixation and spinal‑cord isolation steps.

steps.title: Monitor fluorescence stability
steps.instruction: Note that fluorescence from the dextran tracers remains detectable for at least one month but gradually loses intensity over time as the dyes degrade.

description: In zebrafish, motoneurons can be divided into two main types, primary and secondary, depending on the time of their birth, soma size and position in the spinal cord. Primary motoneurons (pMN) are born first, they have large cell bodies and axons, and occupy a dorsal position in the motor column. Secondary motoneurons (sMN) are born later, they have comparatively smaller cell bodies and axons and reside in the ventral part of the motor column. pMNs are fast and innervate the large white muscles. In adult zebrafish, sMNs are heterogenous and comprise three functional subtypes each selectively innervating either fast, intermediate or slow muscles. This classification results in four distinct motoneuron pools.2,3,4,5,6 These pools are organized somatotopically with a defined location in the motor column that relates to the muscle type they innervate. Slow motoneurons are located ventro-laterally, intermediate motoneurons have a ventro-medial location and fast motoneurons are located medio-dorsally in the spinal motor column. Zebrafish transgenic lines labeling MNs are available, but these do not discriminate among the different MN types due to the lack of specific genetic markers for slow, intermediate and fast MNs. For the analysis of motor circuits, it is necessary to identify and access each MN pool separately, this can only be done through retrograde labeling from specific muscles. In zebrafish, fast, intermediate and slow muscles are spatially segregated, in contrast to mammals where they are intermingled. The zebrafish slow red muscle fibers occupy a thin lateral strip, the intermediate (or pink) form a wedge-shaped area around the horizontal septum, and the white fast fibers represent the large medial portion of the myotome.7,8,9 The spatial segregation of muscles fibers in adult zebrafish allows for precise targeting of each muscle type by injecting dextran tracers to retrogradely label the MNs innervating them.2,3,4,6 Single or multiple MN pools can be labeled
